title: What should one pressure-drop run cover by default?
context: Run time is set by how many Reynolds points, how many flow directions and which grid. Low points are cheap (the lattice fluid stays viscous and settles in a few thousand steps); the top point dominates, because a less viscous lattice fluid settles slowly. Rough figures at 64³ on Matt's RTX (about 27,000 steps a second from the 2026-10-14 bench): Re up to 10 well under 0.2 s a point, Re 20–50 about 1 s, Re 100 about 1.5–3 s with a warm start from the previous point. At 128³ the same top point is one to two minutes. These are estimates for the bench to confirm. The scope (§11.7, 2026-10-07) said to wait for the database user's operating range before fixing defaults; this sets a provisional, editable default and needs no answer from him to start.

options.name: Six points to Re 100, chosen direction, 64³
options.summary: Reynolds numbers 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 (editable list), solved along the Flow direction setting (All = the three axes), on the flow grid. Points above what the grid resolves are skipped with a note; 128³ is allowed with a time warning.
options.sketch: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 180'><line x1='20' y1='120' x2='304' y2='120' stroke='currentColor'/><text x='20' y='140' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>1</text><text x='106' y='140' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>10</text><text x='190' y='140' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>100</text><text x='276' y='140' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>1000</text><text x='162' y='166' font-size='12' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>Reynolds number</text><rect x='20' y='92' width='175' height='16' fill='var(--good)' opacity='0.35'/><text x='26' y='86' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>64³ resolves</text><circle cx='45' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--accent)'/><circle cx='79' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--accent)'/><circle cx='105' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--accent)'/><circle cx='131' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--accent)'/><circle cx='165' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--accent)'/><circle cx='190' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--accent)'/><text x='230' y='40' font-size='11' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>about 10–20 s</text><text x='230' y='56' font-size='11' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>all three axes</text></svg>
pros: Fits the 10–20 s budget: about 3–6 s per direction, 10–20 s with All, plus the wall links Flow already builds.
Dense where inertia switches on (Re about 2–20), which is where the inertia-onset number and the fit's quality are decided.
Covers Castro et al.'s 29–145 except its top, and the bottom half of the heat-exchanger range.
A heat exchanger has a known flow direction, so one axis is often all a user needs (3× faster).
cons: Stops at Re 100: the upper heat-exchanger range (200–500) needs 128³ and minutes per design.
Six points, not the scope's five; the list differs from the 2026-10-07 draft.

options.summary: Reynolds numbers 1, 10, 50, 100 and 200 as written in the scope, on every open axis, with Re 200 on a 128³ grid.

pros: Matches the scope as written in 2026-10-07.
Reaches Re 200, further into the heat-exchanger range.
cons: Re 200 on all three axes at 128³ is several minutes per design: outside the 10–20 s budget.
Only one point (Re 1–10) where inertia switches on, so the onset number is poorly placed.
Re 1 adds nothing the creeping-flow run does not already give.

options.name: Automatic to what the grid resolves
options.summary: No list: points spaced evenly on a log scale from Re 1 up to the highest Reynolds number the chosen grid resolves for that design (about 100 at 64³, about 400 at 128³), on every open axis.
options.sketch: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 180'><line x1='20' y1='120' x2='304' y2='120' stroke='currentColor'/><text x='20' y='140' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>1</text><text x='106' y='140' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>10</text><text x='190' y='140' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>100</text><text x='276' y='140' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>1000</text><text x='162' y='166' font-size='12' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>Reynolds number</text><rect x='20' y='72' width='175' height='14' fill='var(--good)' opacity='0.35'/><text x='200' y='83' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>64³</text><rect x='20' y='96' width='226' height='14' fill='var(--accent)' opacity='0.35'/><text x='250' y='107' font-size='11' fill='currentColor'>128³</text><text x='160' y='40' font-size='11' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>range follows the grid and design</text></svg>
pros: Nothing to set: every design gets the widest range its grid supports.
The top point is always one the grid can resolve.
cons: Designs in a sweep end up on different Reynolds points, so columns at a fixed Re need interpolation.
All axes at 128³ runs into minutes per design.
Less predictable for a user who wants a specific operating point.
options.effort: Same build plus a grid-cap estimate per design.

recommendation: It keeps a normal Lab run inside the 10–20 s budget, puts its points where inertia switches on, and leaves Re 200 and above as a deliberate, slower 128³ choice. Confirm with the bench numbers before building.
